still_true: Wegovy's US list price is still $1,349 a month on the branded box, and almost nobody pays it.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, and oral Wegovy starting doses still cost $149 a month there.

The September 2027 tri-agency guidance allowing up to 30% premium differentials tied to verified adherence still stands, and Illinois's ban on adherence-conditioned premiums is still the only state ban in force.
The suicidal-ideation warning is still off the labels of every incretin, branded and generic.
DOT still has not ruled on off-label alcohol-reduction incretin use among commercial drivers, and the Army recruit oral pilot continues without expansion.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Arithmetic: 33.0% ever-used minus 24.7% current = 8.3% of adults who used and are off now. 44% of 33.0 = 14.5 points cycled: ~12.4 points are current users on at least a second course (~50% of current users, diluted by 2032's first-time generic and Medicare starters) and ~2.1 points cycled and are off again. The other ~6.2 points stopped once and have not restarted. New ever-users in the window = 7.5 points (~20M people). One-year persistence rose from about a third to about 40%, driven by $0 generic copays and monthly dosing. Age check: 0.20×13 + 0.33×22.8 + 0.24×34 + 0.23×28 = 2.6 + 7.52 + 8.16 + 6.44 = 24.7. Of ~270M adults, 24.7% is ~66.7M users. FICTIONAL payer mix: Medicare 28% (~18.7M), Medicaid 12% (~8.0M), HRSA free provision at health centres 3.5% (~2.3M), commercial 22% (~14.7M), legitimate cash 28.5% (~19.0M), gray market 6% (~4.0M). Public payers together cover 43.5% (~29M) and are now the default route for new starters. Medicare check: ~17.4M users are 65+ (0.28 × ~62M); ~15.9M of them are on Medicare, joined by ~2.8M disabled under-65 beneficiaries, for ~18.7M. The income gap narrowed sharply (top-to-bottom 27 vs 22, from 23 vs 12) because generics, Medicaid's enhanced match and health-centre provision reached the bottom third. The top third grew least: some of the top tier are visibly quitting (see body_and_culture). Adult obesity ~32.5%. Roughly 19% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug, mostly men under 50 and rural uninsured adults. Pediatric: ~4.2% of 12–17s (~1.05M) and ~0.35% of 6–11s (~85k, still liraglutide only) are on a drug, ~1.5% of under-18s in all. Medicaid EPSDT now carries most new adolescent starts.

access.public_coverage: Since Jan 2032 Medicare Part D covers anti-obesity medication for adults with BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a comorbidity, under the Dec 2031 Metabolic Health Access provisions. Generic semaglutide comes first, with a $0 copay. Branded agents require step therapy or a diabetes/CV/CKD/OSA/dementia-risk code. To stay covered on the obesity-only route, users must show ≥5% weight loss or maintenance at 6 months. FICTIONAL arithmetic: Medicare ~18.7M users. ~10.3M are on generic semaglutide at ~$45 net/month × 12 = ~$5.6B, and ~8.4M are on branded agents at ~$230 net × 12 = ~$23.2B, for ~$28.7B a year. That is roughly flat against 2030's $29.7B for 9.9M users. Medicaid: a 90% federal match for generic incretins brought coverage to 31 states plus DC. ~8.0M users: ~6.8M generic at ~$40 × 12 = ~$3.3B, plus ~1.2M branded at ~$245 × 12 = ~$3.5B, for ~$6.8B. HRSA free provision: ~2.3M patients × ~$38 acquisition × 12 = ~$1.05B, inside a $1.1B annual grant.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide is $4–30 a month, and Indian FDA-inspected plants (Dr. Reddy's, Sun, Biocon) now also supply US ANDAs. Chinese tirzepatide-analogues sell across Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa. Canadian generics are CAD 40–70. India and China make most of the world's incretin volume and most US generic API.
access.note: FICTIONAL. The semaglutide compound patent and its extension expired in Dec 2031. Six generic injectable semaglutide makers plus Novo's authorised generic launched between Jan and Sep 2032. Cash prices fell from ~$129 at launch to $39–69 a month by Oct 2032 at Costco, Cost Plus and Walmart. Generic oral semaglutide is blocked by absorption-enhancer patents. Branded prices held but bent: TrumpRx Wegovy pill starts at $149 with maintenance at $229; Zepbound cash is $249–299; Foundayo $129–229; MariTide $199 cash ($1,180 list); retatrutide $1,299 list. Tirzepatide is brand-only until the mid-2030s. Employer coverage rose 36% → 41% on generic-first designs, and pharmacy trend fell. Monitored metabolic tracks hold ~5.8M enrollees, all within the ~14.7M commercial users, ~4M of them on clinic-administered MariTide. Orals fell to ~36% of users. Generic weekly semaglutide (~25M users) is now the single largest product. MariTide has ~6M users. The gray market shrank to ~4M: research-grade retatrutide, microdosers, people avoiding records, people without prescriptions, and some under-18s.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, and US generics since Jan 2032)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1/amylin co-agonist, weekly injectable (amycretin, approved Nov 2030)
GLP-1 agonist/GIP-receptor antagonist antibody conjugate, monthly injectable (MariTide; clinic-administered and, since Jul 2031, home autoinjector)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: adolescent obesity 12+ (semaglutide incl. generics, liraglutide, Wegovy pill)
reduction of risk of all-cause dementia in adults with obesity and established CVD (tirzepatide; the extension to 60+ without CVD got a complete response letter in May 2031)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol reduction via telehealth and EAPs (oral semaglutide AUD phase 3 read out positive in 2031; filed, no decision before 2033)
dementia-prevention use by 50–70-year-olds without CVD, now mostly on cheap generic semaglutide instead of tirzepatide
microdosing for 'steadiness', now more often for social-drinking control than for work
semaglutide in under-12s with severe obesity (off-label)
'drug holidays' and self-down-titration on generic pens, now openly coached by telehealth
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. Amycretin, filed Oct 2029, was approved Nov 2030 as a weekly injection with ~22% weight loss; it is mostly on commercial formularies behind step therapy. No new indication was granted in the window. FDA issued a complete response on tirzepatide's dementia extension to adults 60+ without CVD (May 2031), asking for the confirmatory trial readout, now expected 2033. The oral semaglutide AUD sNDA was filed in late 2031, with a decision due 2033. The monthly driver is realised through the existing MariTide in a new form (home autoinjector, Jul 2031) and through employer and Medicare clinic administration. No implant exists; implant programmes remain in phase 1 and are not on the market. No new monthly molecule was filed in time for approval by 2032. The bimagrumab-type muscle adjunct read out phase 3 in 2032; it is not filed and not approved. Tirzepatide and retatrutide face no generic before the mid-2030s. Global incretin market ~$150B by revenue (volume much higher). Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell ~55% in 2032.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Self-titration on cheap generic pens has reduced early GI dropout in some users, but titration errors raise ER visits among new Medicare starters. MariTide early vomiting remains highest.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; severe gastroparesis caution retained across brands and generics.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss. Absolute cholecystectomy volume is up with the Medicare expansion.
Still no causal confirmation; absolute risk low. Litigation now runs mostly on the exocrine theory.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled. New MDL filings cite exocrine insufficiency; no settlement yet.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Hip-fracture HR holds at ~1.3 in users 65+ after >2 years, and ~1.45 in those who have cycled three or more times. The Medicare expansion roughly doubled the number of exposed older users, so absolute fracture counts are rising even though the hazard ratio is unchanged.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning retained on generic labels. The Part D obesity benefit pays for a baseline DXA but not for resistance-training programmes.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Conflicting cohorts; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Listed in adverse reactions; no class warning.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Clinically meaningful anhedonia still ~7–8% of users vs ~3% of controls, ~10% on retatrutide. Interim data from the FDA observational study (2032) confirm the dose relationship. No randomised data.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing study continues. No labelling, though professional guidance now endorses dose reduction for flattening.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months, worse after repeated cycles. Medicare's 6-month continuation criterion has created a new group of non-responders who lose coverage and then regain.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. It underpins the chronic-therapy framing and the continuation criteria.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: B12, iron and vitamin D deficiency are documented in low-intake users. Fat-soluble deficiency is linked to the exocrine signal.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added micronutrient monitoring language to semaglutide labels in 2031. Annual panels are covered under the Part D benefit's companion Part B codes.

safety_ledger.effect: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency after 5+ years of continuous use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Danish and Optum rates are unchanged (~4.1 vs ~1.9 per 1,000 person-years after 5+ years). Partial reversal after stopping appears in small follow-ups. Tirzepatide data beyond 5 years remain thin. Generic launch means the longest-exposed users are now on the cheapest product.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added an EPI statement to Warnings and Precautions for semaglutide products, including generics, in 2031. Class labelling for other agents is still undecided. EMA PRAC recommended monitoring.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; effects in adolescents and children on drug for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of semaglutide follow-up now exist. Pediatric bone interim data (liraglutide 6–11) show no growth deficit at 2 years but are underpowered. Under-18 exposure grew ~40% in the window, mostly through generic semaglutide in Medicaid.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric postmarketing requirements continue. No new requirements are attached to generic ANDAs.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Counterfeit-pen incidents fell as legal prices dropped below gray-market prices. Research-grade retatrutide remains the main overdose source. A 2032 FDA warning letter to one Indian ANDA plant over particulates triggered a voluntary recall of ~400k generic pens, with no confirmed injuries. Poison-centre calls are ~3× 2025 levels, down from ~4×.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alert on finished pens retained. FDA added foreign-inspection capacity for incretin ANDA sites, and serialisation extended to generics.

food_and_beverage.state: About 42% of US households now have a user. Snack and confectionery volumes are down ~11% from 2025 and sugary drinks ~9%. The class split is inverting: lower-income zip codes, newly medicated through Medicaid and health centres, are where value-pack volumes now fall fastest. Premium 'full-flavour' and indulgence lines (butter, heritage pastry, whole-milk dairy) grow among upper-income buyers who market themselves as unmedicated. Protein ingredient prices have eased as capacity came on.

alcohol.state: Spirits volumes are down ~13% from 2025 and beer ~8%. Heavy-drinker erosion now reaches lower-income markets via cheap generics. Craft and premium wine hold up in upper-income metros, where drinking is part of the 'unmedicated' signal. Bar closures continue in mid-sized Midwestern and Southern cities.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat to slightly down. Value-menu QSR growth stalled as lower-income use rose. Upper-tier tasting menus and 'appetite' dinners (large-format, communal, multi-course) in New York, Los Angeles and Austin are booked out. Casual dining still runs smaller checks and protein bowls.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting. 'Structured' athleisure for lean bodies is now mass-market and discounted. Premium labels pivoted to 'full-cut' tailoring and softer silhouettes for bodies that signal they are not medicated. Resale serves cyclers.

fitness.state: Strength training keeps growing. DXA scans are now cheap and covered for Medicare starters, so the premium clubs moved on to 'vitality' coaching: VO2 max, grip strength, appetite and sleep. Budget gyms report record sign-ups among new Medicaid and Medicare users told to lift.

insurance.state: Employer coverage recovered to 41% on generic-first designs, and pharmacy trend fell to ~+3% in 2032. Adherence differentials persist under the 2027 guidance. Several large employers quietly removed 'steadiness' competency language after the EEOC finding but kept verification. Part D premiums rose again for 2033, though less than feared, because generics carry most of the new obesity-only volume.

pharma.state: Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell ~55% in 2032 as generics took ~70% of semaglutide volume. Lilly (tirzepatide, retatrutide) and Amgen (MariTide) grew. Teva, Viatris-Biocon, Dr. Reddy's and Sun split a high-volume, low-margin US generic market. Denmark's growth forecast was cut, partly on Novo.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A lean body no longer signals much. It is what a $0 Medicare copay or a $39 pen produces, and it reads as ordinary, possibly subsidised. The scarce body is 'unmedicated vitality': visible muscle with some softness, colour in the face, a full plate eaten in public. In upper-income circles the important fact is whether you are on the drug, not how much you weigh. A regained body over 50 now reads less as lost coverage and more as a failed continuation check.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The inversion is clearest among upper-income women aged 30–49 in Austin and Brooklyn. Some are tapering off and accepting a few kilos as the price of being visibly unmedicated. Some quietly stay on low doses while claiming to be off, which the scene calls 'ghosting'. In Charlotte banking, DXA printouts went out of fashion within a year and grip-strength and VO2 numbers replaced them. On the Columbus logistics corridor and in Medicaid-expansion counties of Kentucky, the thin, soft body is now the majority body and carries no particular stigma. Bottom-third women 50–64 who regained in 2030 are, in large numbers, back on generic semaglutide.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: In upper-tier homes, serving a rich, long meal is a statement, and dessert is back as a status course. In lower-income homes, shared meals have shortened the way they did for the upper tier five years ago. 'Bread Alone' fasting congregations number ~600, though their argument (fasting as the discipline the poor can afford) weakened once the drug became free. They now frame fasting as freedom from the state's medicine. School lunch debates turned to adolescents on Medicaid-covered semaglutide.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Bumble's 'unmedicated' tag (Sep 2032) is self-declared, and scan chains sell an optional blood test that verifies it. It became a status marker in New York, LA and Austin within weeks and drew ridicule elsewhere. 'Lean-mass verified' badges declined. Desire mismatch is still the most common complaint in couples therapy, and couples now plan around the monthly shot date or a shared 'long month' without it.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Among the affluent, appetite has become a luxury: proof that you do not need to manage yourself chemically. In subsidised communities appetite is treated as a symptom the clinic handles. Unmuted claims the inversion as vindication while complaining that the rich took over its aesthetic. MAHA-adjacent influencers sell 'natural vitality' supplements to exactly the people who just got the drug free.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Clinically meaningful anhedonia is still ~7–8% of users vs ~3% of controls, ~10% on retatrutide. In a 2032 KFF poll, ~31% of current users reported a planned drug holiday or self-directed dose reduction in the past year, most often to feel 'more like myself', for a trip, or for sex. Among monthly users, ~22% reported deliberately skipping a month.
interior_life.framing: Mostly called a side effect you manage: 'turning it down'. Telehealth firms market 'holiday protocols'. HR has largely stopped calling it steadiness in writing since the 2032 EEOC finding, though shift supervisors still use the word. Unmuted calls the affluent taper an aesthetic that only people with good coverage and a safety net can afford.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Metabolic tracks hold ~5.8M enrollees, and clinic-administered MariTide still makes adherence a recorded fact. After the EEOC's reasonable-cause finding against a Columbus-corridor logistics firm, which settled, written competency language disappeared from most large employers. Verification and premium differentials remain. Workers in tracks now negotiate 'documented dose reductions' with clinic nurses rather than holidays, because a skipped dose shows up in the adherence record. Upper-tier white-collar staff take open holidays. Some list 'unmedicated' on personal websites.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Unmuted 'off nights' went mainstream and partly commercial, with ticketed events in Austin and Brooklyn drawing the affluent tapering crowd. The original Detroit and Baltimore nights resent this. 'Flat' fiction gave way to 'holiday' memoirs about the week the feeling came back. Sportsbook wagering per account fell further as cheap generics reached lower-income heavy bettors. Comedy about Medicare continuation weigh-ins is a staple.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Planned holidays around anniversaries and conception are common and openly discussed with clinicians. Monthly users plan 'long months'. Some couples are on different routes, one on the free generic and one tapering off for status, and therapists report that mismatch now runs along class aspiration as well as desire.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Both parties claimed the Dec 2031 Metabolic Health Access provisions during the 2032 campaign, the Republican line as 'generic-first savings' and the Democratic line as 'coverage'. The MAHA wing opposed the subsidy and lost. The anti-adherence-premium coalition revived slightly after the EEOC finding but passed no new state laws. 'Sedated electorate' claims still have no turnout evidence. The medicated-versus-regained zip-code split blurred as Medicaid and health centres reached regainers.

state.regulatory_posture: FDA kept its pro-speed posture: amycretin approved, ANDAs approved promptly at patent expiry, and the MariTide autoinjector cleared. It also turned down the dementia extension pending confirmatory data and added EPI language to semaglutide labels. It increased foreign inspections of generic plants. No new state action on adherence premiums.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: The Dec 2031 year-end package (Metabolic Health Access provisions) created a Part D obesity benefit from Jan 2032: generic-first step therapy, $0 copay for generic semaglutide, and continuation criteria. It set a 90% federal Medicaid match for generic incretins and created a $1.1B a year HRSA grant for free generic semaglutide at federally qualified health centres. It does not mandate use and does not change the 2027 premium guidance.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Medicare's 6-month continuation criterion makes weight a coverage condition for ~6.5M obesity-only beneficiaries. Health centres record weigh-ins in the grant reporting system. Employer verification via clinic administration records continues under consent forms, and two state Medicaid programmes still condition coverage on adherence and BMI progress.
state.workforce_or_military: TRICARE added generic semaglutide for obesity under the same package. The Army recruit oral pilot continues without expansion. DOT has still not ruled on alcohol-reduction use among drivers.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US generic semaglutide depends heavily on Indian API and fill-finish. The 2032 particulate recall at one Indian plant briefly tightened supply and gave the import-enforcement debate a new angle: the cheap legal supply and the gray supply come from the same country. Novo's US revenue drop reached Danish fiscal forecasts, and Copenhagen now asks Washington about tariffs rather than about price gaps.

events.event: FDA approves Novo Nordisk's amycretin, a weekly GLP-1/amylin co-agonist, for chronic weight management at ~22% labelled weight loss; it launches at a $1,249 list price behind commercial step therapy

FDA issues a complete response letter on Lilly's bid to extend tirzepatide's dementia-risk claim to adults 60+ without heart disease, citing the pending confirmatory trial and fracture risk in the target population
FDA approves a home-use monthly autoinjector for Amgen's MariTide; Amgen cuts its direct cash price to $199, while large employers keep metabolic-track enrollees on clinic-administered doses

Congress's year-end package, rescored after generic semaglutide approvals cut projected costs, creates a Part D obesity benefit with $0 generic copays and 6-month continuation criteria, a 90% Medicaid match for generic incretins, and a $1.1B HRSA free-provision grant for health centres

Generic semaglutide launches in the US after the compound patent expires, from Teva, Viatris-Biocon, Dr. Reddy's, Sun and a Novo authorised generic; by October, cash prices at Costco and Cost Plus reach $39–69 a month

EEOC issues a reasonable-cause finding in an ADA charge against a Columbus-corridor logistics firm over 'even under pressure' competency language tied to metabolic-track enrolment; the firm settles and several national employers drop similar wording

open_tensions: Public money now pays to keep ~29M Americans on incretins for decades, generic-first, with older beneficiaries carrying the fracture warning. Children's exposure is growing through Medicaid. The EPI signal on long-term semaglutide is labelled but not understood, and the longest-exposed users are now on the cheapest product.

The affluent are turning 'unmedicated vitality' into a status marker just as the drug becomes a subsidised public-health default. That risks stigmatising the subsidised body and makes tapering, regain and 'ghosting' a class performance that the health-centre and Medicare populations cannot afford to copy.

Medicare's 6-month continuation criterion and employers' clinic-recorded adherence make weight and compliance conditions of coverage. Drug holidays are now mainstream medical advice, but for the verified population a holiday is a recorded lapse, and the 2027 premium guidance still stands.

Tirzepatide, retatrutide and MariTide remain branded at $199–1,299 cash while semaglutide costs $39. The dementia extension awaits a 2033 readout, US generic supply depends on a few Indian plants, and Denmark's economy is absorbing Novo's US revenue collapse.

prose.headline: Free, Thin and Out of Fashion: Medicare Pays for the Pen as the Rich Start Eating Dessert Again
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 one American adult in four takes an incretin drug, and a third have tried one. The jump came from the calendar. In December 2031 the semaglutide compound patent expired. Within weeks generic pens from Teva, Viatris and two Indian makers were on pharmacy shelves, and Novo sold its own authorised generic beside them. By autumn a month of the drug that once listed at $1,349 cost $39 at Costco. The branded box still carries the old price, and nobody pays it.

The cheaper drug changed the politics. A Medicare obesity benefit had been scored for years as too expensive to pass. Rescored against generic prices, it went through in the December year-end package. Since January, Medicare beneficiaries with obesity can get generic semaglutide for nothing, provided they have lost or kept off five percent of their weight by the six-month check. Medicaid's federal match for generic incretins rose to ninety percent, and thirty-one states took it. Community health centres received a billion dollars a year to hand the pens out free. Public programmes now cover more users than any other payer. Medicare's incretin bill is roughly what it was in 2030, for nearly twice the people.

The income gap closed faster than anyone had modelled. Two years ago the top third of earners used the drugs at twice the rate of the bottom third. Now the figures are twenty-seven percent and twenty-two. Gray-market vials lost most of their reason to exist, although research-grade retatrutide still moves through social shops and still sends people to emergency rooms. Lilly's tirzepatide and retatrutide and Amgen's monthly MariTide remain branded and expensive, and they are now the drugs of good insurance. MariTide got a home autoinjector, but the warehouses outside Columbus still give it at the plant clinic, where the dose goes into a record.

In March the EEOC found reasonable cause in a complaint against one of those warehouses over competency language that rewarded being 'even under pressure.' The company settled, and the word steadiness disappeared from a great many HR documents. The monitoring stayed. What changed is that the flattening is now something people say out loud. Almost a third of users told pollsters they had taken a planned break or turned their own dose down in the past year. Telehealth companies sell holiday protocols. Couples plan a 'long month' without the monthly shot. The anhedonia numbers have not moved: about one user in thirteen.

The safety ledger held. No new signal appeared. The exocrine pancreas warning went onto semaglutide labels, generics included. The fracture warning matters more as Medicare enrols millions of older users. The FDA declined Lilly's request to widen the dementia claim and asked for the trial first.

The largest change is in what bodies mean. When a lean body cost a good job and a scan membership, it signalled money. When it costs nothing at a health centre in Hazard, Kentucky, it signals very little. In Austin and Brooklyn, women who were early adopters are tapering off and accepting a few kilos to be seen eating. Some stay on small doses and say they are off; their friends call it ghosting. Grip strength replaced lean-mass percentages at Charlotte dinner parties. Bumble added an 'unmedicated' tag, and a scan chain sells a blood test to prove it. Butter and whole-milk brands are growing in upscale grocers. Value-pack snacks are falling fastest in the zip codes that were medicated last.

Both presidential campaigns took credit for the free pen. Denmark cut its growth forecast. From a distance the country looks thinner again, calmer again, and newly uneasy about which of those it wants to be seen as.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Darlene Pruitt is at the Kroger pharmacy in Dayton by eight, because the weigh-in kiosk is shortest before the shift change. She takes off her shoes. The kiosk reads 6.8 percent down from February, and the printout calls it a CONTINUATION ELIGIBLE RESULT. She folds it twice and puts it in her coat with the Medicare card.

The pens are generic now, a white box with a Teva logo and a sticker that says $0.00. The pharmacist reminds her about the bone scan she has scheduled and keeps not going to. Darlene says Thursday.

At eleven she drives to her son's to watch Kaylee, who is fifteen and on the same pen through Medicaid. Kaylee doesn't want to talk about it. She wants to talk about a girl at school whose mother is 'off,' and who brings croissants for everyone on Fridays.

Lunch is half a turkey sandwich. Darlene wraps the other half in foil for later, knowing she won't eat it.

Her daughter-in-law calls from Charlotte at three, from a restaurant, loud. She has stopped her shot, she says, for the summer, maybe longer. She says she feels hungry, and she sounds like she's bragging. In the background someone is ordering a second dessert for the table.

After dinner Kaylee asks what it was like before, when you could just want things. Darlene thinks about it. She says it was mostly the same, only louder.

At nine she sets the alarm for Sunday's injection. The foil package is still in the fridge.
